utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court) Good afternoon everybody. Mr. Prosecutor, we will not have to issue a binding order on the witness. I hope he is here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: First of all, an apology on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I am sorry for wasting the court's time. He has been rushed here. He is outside, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let us have him brought in and we will work until three o'clock. We will not delay the following hearing. We will try to break, however, at a proper point. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the cross-examination. Good afternoon, Colonel. How are you today? Are you feeling all right? As all military men should be. We will now continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Hayman, you may proceed. LIEUTENANT-COLONEL LANDRY (continued) Cross-examined by MR HAYMAN (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. Lieutenant-Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to your visit to the village of Skradno, which I believe was between the January and April conflicts in 1993. Can you tell us what month your first visit was to Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could have just a moment to find the information in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take all the time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps while the Lieutenant-Colonel is checking his notes, we could activate the ELMO and focus on the map which has been placed on the ELMO. Mr. President, it is a standard former JNA or JNA 1 to 50,000 map, with which we have all become acquainted, of the Lasva Valley area. Lieutenant-Colonel, have you found an entry that is pertinent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first entry is dated 21st March. I have other entries as well. I think that the last time I was there was in June or in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to the ELMO to your right and indicate -- perhaps with the pointer -- the village of Skradno. If I can help you, it is above, to the north-east of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating the village of Skradno. Can you tell us where that village lay in relationship to the front-line between the HVO and the BiH army when you visited in March, March 21st, 1993? Was it far from the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the main road, connecting Zenica, I think that the contact point on the road, which was under Bosnian control, was about here. (Indicating on map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did the front-line come to the south between Skradno and Merdani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been somewhere here, in this region. As I have said, I worked a great deal in the Donji and Gornji region over here. Therefore, I assume, since I did not actually go -- take that road or I suppose that the front-line or the combat line between the two sides, the Croats and the Bosnians must have been somewhere between those two points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the east of Skradno and either south or somewhat south, south-west of Merdani; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is about right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a fence or wire, barbed wire around the village of Skradno when you visited in March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we discussed the presence of guards in or around the village. Were there patrols of guards in or around the village of Skradno when you first visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The only thing that we saw when we were in Skradno was that there was a road which gave access to Skradno. If you are looking at the map you might say there was more than one, but I always went to Skradno using the road that gave access to the main road to Busovaca and the police, as I said yesterday -- they were civilian or HVO police -- were at the junction of that road, just at the point we crossed the river. Either on this side of the river, the Busovaca, or the other side. They are the ones who guarded access to that Muslim enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told by any of the inhabitants whether the guards that you saw at the access point, if you will, to the village, were they responsible for assaults or robberies of the villagers or were they attempting to protect the villagers against such assaults or robberies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police and the -- that is what the police and the HVO said, that they were there in order to ensure the safety of the Skradno inhabitants, given the tensions that prevailed at that time among the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that the villagers themselves described certain robberies or assaults; did they tell you whether the guards were responsible for those events or not? Or were they not responsible and it was someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they told us, and what I think I reported in one of the subsequent reports, is that there were allegations from some individuals who had taken testimonies about what had happened and they told us that they remembered that there was at least one of the people who was dressed in black and wearing a hood, that one of those people apparently was one of the guards who, during the day, was supposed to be there to protect them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the guards you saw dressed in black or were they wearing other types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the information which I have noted down is that I -- that they were HVO police, but I later looked again and realised that was very difficult to distinguish between the military and the civilian police. One day people were wearing a military uniform, the next day people were wearing different clothes, so everything -- everyone in uniform in the HVO sector had to answer to the commands of the HVO authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there an HVO representative present with you in Skradno on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. As I said yesterday, we had received a protest in the morning, in the Commission. It was a common thing. In the afternoon, when we go to investigate the protest, at the part there was a group separated into two parts. I was in one part of the group with a representative from the Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the other side as well, in order to investigate the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecutor suggested that you keep your answers concise and focus so that the proceedings will move along quickly. I would make the same request. Who accompanied you from the HVO on this visit; if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want me to be succinct, then I am just going to tell you I do not remember. If you want the name of the person, I will have to look at my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not remember, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I can tell you that it was one of the people authorised to sit at the Busovaca Joint Commission, because at no point were investigations made with people who did not have a legitimate position authorised by the Bosnian or HVO authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, excuse me, try to answer -- excuse me, Colonel, I was saying, try to answer the questions that you are asked. If it is necessary for there to be additional comments, the Defence counsel will ask for the additional information or the judges will ask for it later, or the Prosecutor will, if necessary. Thank you, I do understand that you are trying to give very specific answers. Proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do you remember what request or requests you or the other participants of the Commission made of the HVO representative concerning Skradno on or after your visit to Skradno on March 21, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were asked, in brief, to be sure that life could resume its normal course, that is in Skradno, that these people stopped being abused and that they could go into their fields to harvest their crops for things to go back to normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, was there a request that there be more security or less security by whatever police elements were providing some level of security at the entrance to the village? Did you ask that those people leave or that they be reinforced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We simply asked that Skradno not be considered as a prison and that the people be in a position to go about their daily lives, since there was -- there was no -- there was no fighting there. We did not want Skradno to become a prison but to be a place where normal life, normal everyday life could go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You later returned to Skradno and you told us yesterday that the situation improved on your subsequent visits, that is the conditions you found in the village. Can you tell the court how the conditions in Skradno had improved on your subsequent visit or visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation had mainly improved because there was no more violence being committed against the inhabitants in the evenings. You remember yesterday I described how regularly people were taken out of their houses at night and a mock execution was carried out with a mock execution squad. Those things had been done, but when I said things improved -- but I did not say that they had returned to normal. There continued to be thefts of automobiles and people were prevented from going to harvest their hay and the tractors which were theirs which were being driven by a Bosnian Croat in a neighbouring field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you advise Ambassador Thebault that the situation in Skradno required his intervention with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day the Busovaca Joint Commission would draft a report addressed directly to Ambassador Thebault. Every day we would receive on average 10 or even 15 protests on some days, relating to incidents having to do with violations of the cease-fire. Therefore, we could not do it -- write a detailed report to Mr. Thebault for each of these incidents but that the representatives of both of the factions, either the HVO or the Bosnians, we told them about the protest, we investigated it, then those people were subsequently to come back to us to give us reports on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that there were so many protests on both sides handled by the Busovaca Joint Commission that the ECMM, and Ambassador Thebault in particular, had to be judicious regarding how often they might raise an issue with, for example, General Hadzihuseinovic or Colonel Blaskic, because they could not be raising an issue every day with them; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but that is also why, as I said yesterday, why there was a meeting every month, or sometimes weekly or bi-weekly, of the Joint Commission, so that Ambassador Thebault be in a position to be able to say that there was lack of cooperation and that one wanted the cooperation to be better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you believe there was a secret agenda on the part of the HVO to drive Muslims out of the Lasva Valley, but you have not identified specifically who harboured such an agenda. Can you tell us who harboured that agenda, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the programme, as I said yesterday, that is the strategy, mainly came from the central HDZ and HVO authorities and that the activities at that time taking place in Central Bosnia were the same type of activities, same type of provocation that one saw in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still have not named any individuals. Did you ever have a discussion with Colonel Blaskic in which he demonstrated or displayed a desire to drive Muslims from the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that type of a meeting, no. But what I do remember, and I remember it very well, is that Colonel Blaskic asked that all the Croats in Zenica be evacuated in buses so they could take over the vacant houses in the Busovaca and Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will talk about Zenica later. You said you do not remember such a meeting; do you think if you had such a meeting it would be one you would be likely to recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, because I have been -- ever since 1996, I have been preparing myself for this testimony here and had that type of visit -- or had that type of meeting occurred I think I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have a substantive discussion in a personal sense -- you and Colonel Blaskic, sitting down and discussing a substantive topic, on any topic during your tour of duty in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to tell you that on several occasions I tried to meet Colonel Blaskic, but it was very difficult for me to do so because I think that after some point, people did not want me to meet with him. The reason I am telling you this is because I have a very clear recollection of an incident when I came back from a vacation in Canada where I brought back presents for all the people with whom I was working and I wanted to bring a present to Colonel Blaskic, but I was told he was not available and could not meet with me, so I left the gift I had brought for him with his secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sure he thanks you for the gift. My question was: did you ever have a substantive discussion with Colonel Blaskic during your tour of duty in Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that once in a while -- well, the start of my stay I did meet Colonel Blaskic but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a substantive discussion on any topics on that occasion or was it a courtesy call?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hayman, that you have asked that question already. You cannot ask him to go more quickly, then to ask the same questions over again. The question was asked and the question was answered three times, including the one relating to a gift for General Blaskic which he never received. The Tribunal heard that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you name one act by Colonel Blaskic, or one order that he gave, that had as its purpose the driving of Muslims from the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys? Can you name one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember having seen a written order, but, as you remember from what I said yesterday, many, many provocative incidents, many provocative incidents which did contribute to the ethnic cleansing on both sides in that region did occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are accusing Colonel Blaskic of inciting a provocative incident, would you please specify what incident or incidents you are accusing him of personally instigating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a small comment so that I can answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Colonel. Since you were ordered to tell us what your thoughts are, you must do so. This is for the proper understanding of these hearings by the judges and, therefore, it is now the Trial Chamber asking you to explain yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never accused personally Colonel Blaskic of anything. Most of my testimony is based on the responsibility of the military chief of all of Central Bosnia. If Colonel Blaskic is not guilty, I would be pleased for him. I have absolutely nothing against him as an individual. But I can tell you that I saw many, many crimes that were committed and I believe that these crimes were not normal, something just normal that happened in Bosnia. There were people in positions of authority who could have done something in order to prevent them and that my impression during my stay in Bosnia is that the people who were in positions of authority did not do everything they could in order to prevent the loss of life. That is what I have been saying since the beginning. Do not say to me that I am accusing General Blaskic. I have never accused him. The only reason I have decided to come to testify here, your Honour, is simply in order to bring to the attention of the court my own perception of my own stay in Bosnia and to profit from my military experiences in order to make people understand that those people who say they are responsible militarily for something, it is not just in order to go to conferences and to be invited to cocktail parties. There is a responsibility which follows from this and these people -- and I have to tell you that the command in Central Bosnia -- General Blaskic was there long enough in order to be able to do something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have answered the question. You have answered the question Colonel. You answered very clearly. There is no need to add anything further. You do not have to take further position. You have answered and that is what the Trial Chamber wanted to know. I believe the incident is now concluded. An answer has been given. The question has been answered and, therefore, we can say that there was no specific provocative facts, according to you, against General Blaskic. You can move to the next question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just so it is absolutely clear, I understand you to be saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, I would like to say something. Let us not -- so that everything is clear. I understand that procedure, Mr. Hayman. Everything is clear, we do not have to go back. We are not going to go back into polemics which are not necessary. We do not have to say, "in order for everything to be clear"; everything is clear. Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslim refugees were accepted into the Lasva Valley during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left Bosnia in August of 1993, the UNHCR statistics showed that out of a population of 4.2 million -- 4.4 million, about 2.2 million were Bosnians who had been displaced. To give you any further information, when I arrived into -- in the city of Zenica in March, the city of Zenica, according to what I was told, there were about 400,000 people -- 80,000 people, excuse me and that the population of Zenica had practically doubled further to the displaced persons having arrived. So, I suppose that the same situation must have been the case in the cities of Vitez and Busovaca as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am moving to a new subject, Mr. President. I do not know when the court intends to break for the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we have -- my intention was clear, but here I have to change things. If we had begun on time, I wanted to be completed with your cross-examination, we would have gone into the next hearing which is of interest to all of you, then we would have resumed the Colonel's testimony for the questions of the right of reply of the Prosecutor and the judges' questions. Now I turn to you, Mr. Hayman, about how much more time do you need for asking your questions? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would say between two and four hours, depending on the gravity or length of the exchanges. I have a number of documents to show the witness. It is going to take some time because of the opinions and breadth of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your clarification. That allows me to completely change my position. As well as the position of my colleagues. I think I can speak on behalf of them. If you will agree, we will suspend the hearing for about a quarter of an hour. Then we will continue in public session, according to the agenda of our work today. The Colonel remains available to the Tribunal. Of course. The hearing is adjourned. (3.10 pm)
